title: Is a Coffee Maker Worth It? Cost per Cup, Home vs Coffee Shop
excerpt: For a daily coffee drinker, almost always: home-brewed coffee costs well under a dollar a cup, so even a good machine pays for itself in weeks. Here is the math, and which type to buy.
html:
If you buy coffee most days, a coffee maker is one of the few kitchen appliances that pays for itself quickly. A cup brewed at home costs a fraction of a coffee-shop cup, and the machine’s price is covered within weeks for most daily drinkers. Whether it is worth it for you depends on how often you drink coffee, what kind you like and how much convenience matters.

Quick answer: yes, if you drink coffee most days. Drip coffee brewed at home typically costs about 30 to 70 cents a cup, against $3 or more for a plain coffee at a café. Saving about $3.50 a cup, a $100 coffee maker pays for itself in about a month at one cup a day.

How Much Does a Cup of Coffee Cost at Home?

Work it out from your own bag of coffee: divide the price of the bag by the number of cups it makes. A 12-ounce (340 g) bag makes roughly 20 to 24 mugs at a typical strength of about 15 grams of coffee per mug.

Coffee bagCups per bagCost per cup
12 oz bag at $9about 22$0.41
12 oz bag at $12about 22$0.55
12 oz bag at $16 (specialty)about 22$0.73
2 lb can at $20about 60$0.33

These are example prices; use your own. Add a few cents for filters, milk and sugar if you take them.

Home Coffee vs Coffee Shop: Typical Cost per Cup

How you get itTypical cost per cup (US)

Prices vary by city and brand, but the gap is the point: home brewing usually saves $2 to $5 a cup.

How Fast Does a Coffee Maker Pay for Itself?

Assuming you save about $3.50 a cup (a $4 café coffee against 50 cents at home):

Coffee maker costPays for itself at 1 cup a dayAt 2 cups a day
$309 days5 days
$6018 days9 days
$10029 days15 days

Even a premium machine is paid off within a few months by a daily coffee drinker. After that, every cup is a saving.

When a Coffee Maker Isn’t Worth It

  • You drink coffee only now and then. A few cups a week may not justify the counter space; a French press or pour-over cone costs very little.
  • You mostly drink lattes and cappuccinos. A drip machine won’t make them; look at an espresso machine instead.
  • Your coffee is free at work. Then a small single-cup brewer for weekends may be all you need.

Which Type of Coffee Maker Is Worth It?

TypeBest forCost per cup
Drip coffee makerHouseholds and 2+ cups a dayLowest
Single-serve pod machineOne cup at a time, speedHigher (pods)
Pour-over or French pressOccasional drinkers, flavor controlLowest, cheap to buy
Espresso machineLattes and cappuccinos at homeLow, but the machine costs more

For most people a programmable drip coffee maker is the best value: it brews a full pot, keeps cost per cup lowest and needs little effort. If you love espresso drinks, our best espresso machines under $500 guide compares the options, and how an espresso machine works explains the difference.

Tips for Better Coffee at Home

  • Use about 1 gram of coffee to 15 to 17 grams of water, roughly 2 tablespoons per 6-ounce cup, and adjust to taste.
  • Buy whole beans and grind just before brewing for more flavor.
  • Use fresh, filtered water if your tap water tastes of chlorine.
  • Clean the carafe after each use and descale the machine every one to three months, depending on your water.
  • Don’t leave coffee on a hot plate for hours; a thermal carafe keeps it hot without cooking it.

Coffee Maker FAQ

Is it cheaper to make coffee at home?

Yes. Drip coffee at home typically costs 30 to 70 cents a cup, against $2.50 to $4 for a plain coffee at a coffee shop.

How long does a coffee maker last?

Many drip machines last around three to five years; premium models such as the Moccamaster are built to last much longer. Regular descaling helps any machine last.

Are pod machines worth it?

They are worth it for speed and convenience if you drink one cup at a time, but pods cost more per cup than ground coffee.

Is an expensive coffee maker worth it?

If you drink coffee every day, a better machine that brews hotter and more evenly can be worth it, and it still pays for itself within months.

What is the cheapest way to make coffee at home?

A French press or pour-over cone with ground coffee: the equipment is inexpensive and cost per cup is the lowest.
